**(B)** \(\dfrac{h\nu}{c}\)

A photon of radiation of frequency \(\nu\) carries energy \(E = h\nu\). A photon has zero rest mass and always travels with the speed \(c\), so Einstein's special theory of relativity relates its energy and its momentum by

\(E = pc\)

\(\therefore\ p = \dfrac{E}{c} = \dfrac{h\nu}{c}\)

Since \(c = \nu\lambda\) for radiation in vacuum, the same momentum may equally be written as \(p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\).

Dimensional check: \(\dfrac{h\nu}{c}\) has units \(\dfrac{\text{J s} \times \text{s}^{-1}}{\text{m s}^{-1}} = \text{kg m s}^{-1}\), which is a momentum. Of the other three expressions, \(h\nu\) is an energy, \(h\lambda\) has units J s m and \(hE\) has units J\(^{2}\) s, so none of them can be a momentum.

Numerical check: for light of \(5000\ \mathring{A}\), \(\nu = 6 \times 10^{14}\) Hz and \(p = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(6 \times 10^{14})}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 1.326 \times 10^{-27}\) kg m/s, which is exactly \(\dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{5 \times 10^{-7}}\), as the two forms require.

**(D)** \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)

The energy carried by a single photon of radiation of frequency \(\nu\) is

\(E = h\nu\)

For radiation travelling in vacuum the frequency and the wavelength are related by \(c = \nu\lambda\), so

\(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}\)

Substituting this frequency in \(E = h\nu\),

\(\therefore\ E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)

The energy of a photon is therefore inversely proportional to its wavelength: the shorter the wavelength, the more energetic the photon.

Dimensional check: \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\) has units \(\dfrac{\text{J s} \times \text{m s}^{-1}}{\text{m}} = \text{J}\), an energy. Of the other three expressions, \(hc\lambda\) has units J s m\(^{2}\) s\(^{-1}\), \(\dfrac{h\lambda}{c}\) has units J s\(^{2}\) and \(\dfrac{\lambda}{hc}\) has units J\(^{-1}\), so none of them is an energy.

Numerical check: at \(\lambda = 5000\ \mathring{A}\), \(E = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{5000 \times 10^{-10}} = 3.978 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 2.49\) eV, which is of the order expected for a visible photon.
twin: (a) Calculate the energies of photons corresponding to ultraviolet light and red light, given that their wavelengths are 3000 \(\mathring{A}\) and 7000 \(\mathring{A}\) respectively.

**Photoelectric effect.** The photoelectric effect is the phenomenon of emission of electrons from a metal surface when radiation of appropriate frequency is incident on it. Such a surface is called a photosensitive surface and the electrons set free are called photoelectrons.

A metal contains free electrons, but they are held inside it by the barrier at its surface and cannot escape unless enough energy is supplied to them. An electron absorbs one whole photon of the incident radiation in a single act, receiving its entire energy \(h\nu\); if that energy is sufficient to carry the electron across the surface barrier, the electron is emitted. Emission takes place only when the frequency of the incident radiation exceeds a threshold frequency \(\nu_0\) characteristic of the metal, however intense the radiation may otherwise be, and once that condition is met the emission is instantaneous, beginning within about \(10^{-9}\) s.

**(i) Stopping potential.** The stopping potential \(V_0\) is the least value of the retarding (negative) potential applied to the collector at which the photoelectric current becomes zero. At this potential even the fastest photoelectron is turned back just before it reaches the collector, so the work done by that electron against the retarding field equals its maximum kinetic energy:

\(eV_0 = K_{max} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2}\)

The stopping potential depends on the frequency of the incident radiation and on the material of the emitter, and is independent of the intensity of the radiation.

**(ii) Photoelectric work function.** The photoelectric work function \(\phi_0\) of a metal is the minimum energy that must be supplied to a free electron at the surface of that metal to just set it free, that is, to remove it from the surface without giving it any kinetic energy. It is a constant of the metal, and it is the photon energy at the threshold:

\(\phi_0 = h\nu_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}\)

Work functions are conveniently expressed in electronvolt; potassium has \(\phi_0 = 2.3\) eV while gold has \(\phi_0 = 5.1\) eV, so potassium emits under visible light where gold needs ultraviolet.

**(a) Threshold frequency.** The threshold frequency \(\nu_0\) of a metal is the minimum frequency of the incident radiation below which no photoelectric emission takes place from that metal, however intense the radiation may be and however long it is allowed to fall on the surface.

If \(\nu < \nu_0\), not a single electron is emitted; if \(\nu > \nu_0\), electrons are emitted at once, however feeble the radiation is. The threshold frequency is a characteristic of the emitter material alone. The wavelength that goes with it, \(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{c}{\nu_0}\), is called the threshold wavelength, and since a longer wavelength means a smaller frequency, radiation of wavelength greater than \(\lambda_0\) cannot produce emission.

**(b) Photoelectric work function.** The photoelectric work function \(\phi_0\) of a metal is the minimum energy that must be supplied to a free electron at the surface of that metal to just set it free, that is, to remove it from the metal surface without giving it any kinetic energy.

The two quantities are two statements of the same property of the metal, connected by

\(\phi_0 = h\nu_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}\)

so that a metal with a large work function has a high threshold frequency and a short threshold wavelength. The work function is usually expressed in electronvolt, \(1\) eV \(= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J; for potassium \(\phi_0 = 2.3\) eV, giving \(\nu_0 = \dfrac{2.3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} = 5.55 \times 10^{14}\) Hz.

**No. Red light is not necessary for the photoelectric effect, and for the common photosensitive metals red light does not produce it at all.**

What decides whether emission occurs is not the colour of the light but whether one photon carries at least the work function of the emitter. Emission takes place only if

\(h\nu \geq \phi_0\), that is only if \(\lambda \leq \lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0}\)

**Red light is in fact the poorest choice in the visible range.** Red has the longest wavelength of the visible colours, roughly \(6200\ \mathring{A}\) to \(7500\ \mathring{A}\), so its photons carry the least energy of any visible light. For red light of \(7000\ \mathring{A}\),

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{7000 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.84 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 1.78\) eV

The smallest work function among the common metals is that of potassium, \(2.3\) eV, whose threshold wavelength is

\(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{2.3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 5.4 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(= 5400\ \mathring{A}\)

which lies in the green part of the spectrum. Red light, at \(6200\ \mathring{A}\) and beyond, is well past this threshold, so it frees no electron from potassium and still less from gold (\(\phi_0 = 5.1\) eV). Making the red beam brighter does not rescue it, because raising the intensity only increases the number of photons arriving each second while every photon still carries the same insufficient \(1.8\) eV, and one electron absorbs one whole photon in a single collision.

\(\therefore\) radiation of shorter wavelength, such as green, blue, violet or ultraviolet, is what the effect requires; red light would serve only for a photosensitive surface whose work function is below about \(1.8\) eV.

**The arrangement to be drawn.** The circuit diagram shows an evacuated glass tube carrying two electrodes, joined to an external circuit as set out below.

| Part of the diagram | What it is and what it does |
|---|---|
| Evacuated glass tube with a quartz window | Encloses the two electrodes. It is evacuated so that the emitted electrons are not stopped by collisions with air molecules, and the window is of quartz because ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet radiation. |
| Emitter C (cathode) | A plate of the photosensitive metal under study. Monochromatic radiation falls on it through the window and photoelectrons are emitted from it. |
| Collector A (anode) | A metal plate facing the emitter, which collects the photoelectrons and so completes the circuit. |
| Battery with a potential divider and a commutator | Applies a variable potential difference between A and C. The commutator reverses the polarity, so that A can be made either positive (accelerating) or negative (retarding) with respect to C. |
| Voltmeter | Connected across A and C to measure the potential difference between the collector and the emitter. |
| Microammeter | Connected in series in the circuit to measure the photoelectric current, which is very small. |
| Source of monochromatic radiation | Provides the incident light. A filter selects the wavelength, and the intensity is varied by changing the power of the source or its distance from the emitter. |

**How the experiment is performed, and the characteristics it establishes.**

1. **Effect of intensity on the photocurrent.** Keep the frequency of the incident radiation and the accelerating potential fixed, and vary the intensity. The photocurrent is found to be directly proportional to the intensity, showing that the number of photoelectrons emitted per second is proportional to the number of photons falling per second.
2. **Effect of the applied potential.** Keep the frequency and the intensity fixed and raise the accelerating potential. The current increases and then settles at a constant value, the saturation current, at which every emitted electron is reaching the collector. Now reverse the polarity and increase the retarding potential; the current falls and becomes zero at the stopping potential \(V_0\), where

\(eV_0 = K_{max}\)

Repeating this for different intensities of the same frequency gives different saturation currents but the SAME stopping potential, which shows that the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons does not depend on the intensity.
3. **Effect of frequency.** Repeat the measurement of \(V_0\) with radiation of different frequencies at a fixed intensity. The stopping potential is found to increase linearly with frequency, and the graph of \(V_0\) against \(\nu\) is a straight line of slope \(\dfrac{h}{e}\) meeting the frequency axis at the threshold frequency \(\nu_0\). Below \(\nu_0\) no current flows however intense the radiation, and above \(\nu_0\) the current starts within about \(10^{-9}\) s however feeble the radiation.

These observations together are the characteristics of the photoelectric effect, and they are summed up by Einstein's photoelectric equation

\(K_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0\)

which also explains the measured slope, since \(eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0\) gives \(V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}\nu - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\).

**(C)** more than two times its initial value

Let the material have work function \(\phi_0\) and let the incident radiation have frequency \(\nu\). By Einstein's photoelectric equation the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectron is

\(K_1 = h\nu - \phi_0\)

When the frequency is doubled to \(2\nu\), the energy of each photon doubles, but the work function is a property of the metal and is unchanged. Hence

\(K_2 = h(2\nu) - \phi_0 = 2h\nu - \phi_0\)

Compare this with twice the initial kinetic energy:

\(K_2 - 2K_1 = (2h\nu - \phi_0) - 2(h\nu - \phi_0) = \phi_0\)

\(\therefore\ K_2 = 2K_1 + \phi_0\)

The work function of every metal is a positive quantity, so \(K_2 > 2K_1\) always. Only for a hypothetical emitter with \(\phi_0 = 0\) would the kinetic energy exactly double, and it can never merely stay the same or fall short of twice its value.

Numerical check: take \(\phi_0 = 2\) eV and \(h\nu = 3\) eV. Then \(K_1 = 3 - 2 = 1\) eV, while on doubling the frequency \(K_2 = 6 - 2 = 4\) eV, which is four times \(K_1\). Taking instead \(\phi_0 = 1\) eV and \(h\nu = 5\) eV gives \(K_1 = 4\) eV and \(K_2 = 9\) eV, a factor of \(2.25\) - greater than two in both cases, as the algebra requires.

**Definition.** The photoelectric effect is the phenomenon of emission of electrons from a metal surface when radiation of appropriate frequency is incident on it. The surface is called a photosensitive surface and the emitted electrons are called photoelectrons. Emission takes place only when the frequency of the incident radiation exceeds a threshold frequency \(\nu_0\) characteristic of the metal, and it then begins within about \(10^{-9}\) s of the radiation striking the surface.

**The experimental set-up.** The apparatus is an evacuated glass tube containing two electrodes, connected to an external circuit.

1. **The tube.** Two electrodes are sealed into an evacuated glass tube. The tube is evacuated so that the photoelectrons travel from one electrode to the other without being stopped by collisions with air molecules. A window of quartz is provided for the radiation to enter, because ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet radiation and many metals need ultraviolet to emit at all.
2. **The emitter and the collector.** The emitter C is a plate of the photosensitive metal being studied, on which the radiation falls. The collector A is a metal plate placed facing it, which receives the photoelectrons and completes the circuit.
3. **The external circuit.** A battery is joined to A and C through a potential divider, so that the potential difference between the two plates can be varied continuously. A commutator in the circuit reverses the polarity, so the collector may be made positive with respect to the emitter (accelerating the electrons) or negative (retarding them). A voltmeter across A and C reads this potential difference, and a microammeter in series reads the photoelectric current, which is of the order of microampere.
4. **The source.** A source of monochromatic radiation illuminates the emitter through the window. Its frequency is selected by a filter and its intensity is varied by changing the distance or the power of the source, so that the effect of each can be studied separately.

**Working.** Radiation falling on the emitter frees photoelectrons from it. With the collector positive, these electrons are drawn across to it and the microammeter registers a photoelectric current; as the accelerating potential is raised, the current increases and then reaches a constant saturation value at which every emitted electron is being collected. With the collector negative, the electrons are opposed, and at the stopping potential \(V_0\) the current falls to zero, so that

\(eV_0 = K_{max}\)

By varying the intensity, the frequency and the applied potential in turn, this single arrangement yields all the characteristics of the effect: the photocurrent is proportional to the intensity, the stopping potential is independent of the intensity, and the stopping potential rises linearly with the frequency, vanishing at \(\nu_0\).

**Einstein's photoelectric equation.** An electron at the metal surface absorbs one whole photon of energy \(h\nu\) in a single act. Part of that energy is spent in freeing the electron from the surface, and the remainder appears as the kinetic energy of the emitted electron. For an electron leaving from the surface itself the loss is least and the kinetic energy is the greatest possible, so

\(h\nu = \phi_0 + K_{max}\)

\(\therefore\ K_{max} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2} = h\nu - \phi_0\)

**Physical significance of each term.**

| Term | What it stands for |
|---|---|
| \(h\nu\) | The energy of one incident photon, \(h\) being Planck's constant and \(\nu\) the frequency of the incident radiation. It is the whole of the energy that one electron can receive, since an electron absorbs one photon and cannot pool the energy of several. |
| \(\phi_0\) | The photoelectric work function of the emitter: the minimum energy needed to just free an electron from its surface. It is a constant of the metal, and \(\phi_0 = h\nu_0\), where \(\nu_0\) is the threshold frequency. |
| \(K_{max}\) | The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectron, measured experimentally through the stopping potential by \(K_{max} = eV_0\). Electrons that come from below the surface lose more energy on the way out and emerge with less than this. |

The equation is the statement of conservation of energy for the single photon-electron encounter. It shows why emission requires \(\nu \geq \nu_0\), why \(K_{max}\) is fixed by the frequency and not by the intensity, and why raising the intensity increases only the number of photoelectrons.

**Numerical.** Wavelength of the incident light \(\lambda = 4000\ \mathring{A} = 4000 \times 10^{-10}\) m \(= 4 \times 10^{-7}\) m. Take \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s and \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s.

The energy of one incident photon is

\(E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)

\(\therefore\ E = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{4 \times 10^{-7}} = \dfrac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{4 \times 10^{-7}}\)

\(\therefore\ E = 4.97 \times 10^{-19}\) J

In electronvolt, \(E = \dfrac{4.97 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.11\) eV.

Check: \(4000\ \mathring{A}\) lies at the violet end of the visible range, where photon energies run from about \(1.8\) eV for red to about \(3.1\) eV for violet, so \(3.11\) eV is consistent.

**The de Broglie wavelength.** Radiation shows a dual character: interference and diffraction need a wave picture, while the photoelectric effect needs a particle picture in which radiation is a stream of photons, each of energy \(E = h\nu\) and momentum \(p = \dfrac{E}{c} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\). In 1924 de Broglie argued from the symmetry existing in nature that if radiation can behave as particles, then matter in motion may behave as waves. He proposed that a moving material particle has a wave associated with it whose wavelength is given by the same relation as for a photon,

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\)

These waves are called matter waves and \(\lambda\) is the de Broglie wavelength. It is a wavelength of a MOVING particle: a particle at rest has \(p = 0\) and no de Broglie wavelength.

**Expression for the de Broglie wavelength of a material particle.** Consider a particle of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(v\), so that its momentum is

\(p = mv\)

By analogy with the photon relation \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\), the wavelength of the wave associated with the particle is

\(\therefore\ \lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}\)

If instead the kinetic energy \(K\) of the particle is known, then for non-relativistic speeds \(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}\), so \(p = \sqrt{2mK}\) and

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\)

For an electron of charge \(e\) accelerated from rest through a potential difference \(V\), the work done on it becomes its kinetic energy, \(K = eV\), and

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} = \dfrac{1.228}{\sqrt{V \text{ (in volt)}}}\) nm

The wavelength is inversely proportional to the momentum, so it is appreciable only for very light particles. For an electron of a few tens of volt it is a few \(\mathring{A}\), comparable with the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is why the wave nature of the electron can be displayed by crystal diffraction; for an everyday body such as a running student it is about \(10^{-36}\) m and can never be observed.

**Numerical: threshold wavelength for a work function of 4.2 eV.**

Data: \(\phi_0 = 4.2\) eV \(= 4.2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 6.72 \times 10^{-19}\) J, \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s, \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s.

At the threshold the whole of the photon energy is used up in just freeing the electron, so

\(\phi_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}\)

\(\therefore\ \lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{6.72 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(\therefore\ \lambda_0 = \dfrac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{6.72 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.96 \times 10^{-7}\) m

\(\therefore\ \lambda_0 = 2960\ \mathring{A} = 296\) nm

Check: substituting back, \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{2.96 \times 10^{-7}} = 6.72 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 4.2\) eV, the given work function. The value lies in the ultraviolet, which is consistent with a work function of \(4.2\) eV being well above the \(1.8\) eV to \(3.1\) eV carried by visible photons.

**(D)** \(2.0\) V

The stopping potential \(V_0\) is the least retarding potential at which the photoelectric current falls to zero. At that potential the fastest photoelectron is just turned back before reaching the collector, so the work it does against the retarding field is exactly its maximum kinetic energy:

\(eV_0 = K_{max}\)

\(\therefore\ V_0 = \dfrac{K_{max}}{e}\)

Here \(K_{max} = 2\) eV \(= 2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 3.2 \times 10^{-19}\) J, so

\(\therefore\ V_0 = \dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.0\) V

The maximum kinetic energy expressed in electronvolt and the stopping potential expressed in volt are numerically equal, because one electronvolt is by definition the energy gained by one electronic charge in falling through one volt. A retarding potential of \(0.5\) V, \(1.0\) V or \(1.5\) V would each still leave some electrons energetic enough to reach the collector, so the current would not have vanished.

**Data:** stopping potential \(V_0 = 1.5\) V; charge on the electron \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C.

At the stopping potential the most energetic photoelectron is just brought to rest before it reaches the collector, so the whole of its kinetic energy is spent as work against the retarding field:

\(K_{max} = eV_0\)

\(\therefore\ K_{max} = (1.6 \times 10^{-19})(1.5)\)

\(\therefore\ K_{max} = 2.4 \times 10^{-19}\) J

In electronvolt,

\(K_{max} = \dfrac{2.4 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.5\) eV

Check: the maximum kinetic energy in electronvolt must come out numerically equal to the stopping potential in volt, since one electronvolt is the energy an electronic charge gains in falling through one volt, and \(1.5\) V has indeed given \(1.5\) eV.

**Data:** work function \(\phi_0 = 2.3\) eV \(= 2.3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 3.68 \times 10^{-19}\) J; wavelength of incident light \(\lambda = 6800\ \mathring{A} = 6800 \times 10^{-10}\) m \(= 6.8 \times 10^{-7}\) m; \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s; \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s; \(1\) eV \(= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J.

**Threshold frequency.** The work function is the energy of a photon at the threshold, so \(\phi_0 = h\nu_0\).

\(\nu_0 = \dfrac{\phi_0}{h} = \dfrac{3.68 \times 10^{-19}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}\)

\(\therefore\ \nu_0 = 5.55 \times 10^{14}\) Hz

**Incident frequency.**

\(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{6.8 \times 10^{-7}}\)

\(\therefore\ \nu = 4.41 \times 10^{14}\) Hz

**Will photoelectrons be emitted?** Here \(\nu = 4.41 \times 10^{14}\) Hz is LESS than \(\nu_0 = 5.55 \times 10^{14}\) Hz, so each incident photon carries less energy than the work function of the metal.

\(\therefore\) there will be NO emission of photoelectrons.

Each photon of the incident light carries only \(E = h\nu = (6.63 \times 10^{-34})(4.41 \times 10^{14}) = 2.925 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 1.83\) eV, which falls \(0.47\) eV short of the \(2.3\) eV needed to free an electron. Since one electron absorbs one whole photon and cannot accumulate energy from several, making the \(6800\ \mathring{A}\) light more intense or leaving it on for longer produces no emission at all. Check by wavelength: the threshold wavelength is \(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{c}{\nu_0} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{5.55 \times 10^{14}} = 5.41 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(= 5405\ \mathring{A}\), and the incident \(6800\ \mathring{A}\) is longer than \(\lambda_0\), which is the same conclusion.

answer:
**Data:** work function of potassium \(\phi_K = 2.25\) eV; work function of caesium \(\phi_{Cs} = 2.14\) eV; wavelength of incident light \(\lambda = 5180\ \mathring{A} = 5180 \times 10^{-10}\) m \(= 5.18 \times 10^{-7}\) m; \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s; \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s; \(1\) eV \(= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J.

The photoelectric effect is possible from a metal only if the energy of one incident photon is at least the work function of that metal. The incident radiation is the same in both cases, so its photon energy need be found only once:

\(E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)

\(\therefore\ E = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{5.18 \times 10^{-7}} = \dfrac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{5.18 \times 10^{-7}}\)

\(\therefore\ E = 3.84 \times 10^{-19}\) J

In electronvolt,

\(\therefore\ E = \dfrac{3.84 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.40\) eV

**Potassium.** \(E = 2.40\) eV is greater than \(\phi_K = 2.25\) eV, so the photoelectric effect IS possible. The fastest electrons emerge with

\(K_{max} = E - \phi_K = 2.40 - 2.25 = 0.15\) eV \(= 2.4 \times 10^{-20}\) J

**Caesium.** \(E = 2.40\) eV is greater than \(\phi_{Cs} = 2.14\) eV, so the photoelectric effect IS possible here as well, with

\(K_{max} = E - \phi_{Cs} = 2.40 - 2.14 = 0.26\) eV \(= 4.16 \times 10^{-20}\) J

\(\therefore\) emission occurs from both metals, and the caesium photoelectrons are the faster of the two because caesium has the smaller work function.

Check by threshold wavelength, \(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0}\): for potassium \(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{2.25 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 5525\ \mathring{A}\) and for caesium \(\lambda_0 = 5809\ \mathring{A}\). The incident \(5180\ \mathring{A}\) is shorter than both thresholds, which agrees with the answers above.
twin: The threshold wavelength of tungsten is \(2.76 \times 10^{-5}\) cm. (b) What will be the maximum kinetic energy of electrons ejected in each of the following cases.

answer:
**Data:** speed of the electron \(v = \dfrac{c}{5} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{5} = 6 \times 10^{7}\) m/s; mass of the electron \(m = 9 \times 10^{-31}\) kg; \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s. Relativistic effects are to be neglected, so the momentum is taken as \(p = mv\).

The de Broglie wavelength of a moving material particle is

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}\)

The momentum of the electron is

\(p = mv = (9 \times 10^{-31})(6 \times 10^{7}) = 5.4 \times 10^{-23}\) kg m/s

\(\therefore\ \lambda = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{5.4 \times 10^{-23}}\)

\(\therefore\ \lambda = 1.228 \times 10^{-11}\) m

\(\therefore\ \lambda = 0.1228\ \mathring{A} = 1.228 \times 10^{-2}\) nm

Check: multiplying back, \(\dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{1.228 \times 10^{-11}} = 5.4 \times 10^{-23}\) kg m/s, which is the momentum found above. The value is about one tenth of the \(1\ \mathring{A}\) belonging to a \(150\) eV electron, as it should be, since this electron moves far faster and \(\lambda\) is inversely proportional to the momentum.
twin: Calculate the wavelength associated with an electron, its momentum and speed (a) when it is accelerated through a potential of 54 V, (b) when it is moving with kinetic energy of 150 eV.

answer:
**(A)** \(0.50\ \mathring{A}\)

For a non-relativistic electron of kinetic energy \(E\), the momentum is \(p = \sqrt{2mE}\), so the de Broglie wavelength is

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mE}}\)

Both \(h\) and the electron mass \(m\) are the same for the two electrons, so

\(\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{E}}\), that is \(\dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{E_1}{E_2}}\)

Here \(E_1 = 150\) eV with \(\lambda_1 = 10^{-10}\) m \(= 1\ \mathring{A}\), and \(E_2 = 0.60\) keV \(= 600\) eV.

\(\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{150}{600} = \dfrac{1}{4}\)

\(\therefore\ \lambda_2 = \lambda_1\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{2} = \dfrac{1\ \mathring{A}}{2}\)

\(\therefore\ \lambda_2 = 0.50\ \mathring{A}\)

Quadrupling the energy halves the wavelength, so the answer must be smaller than \(1\ \mathring{A}\), which already rules out \(1.2\ \mathring{A}\) and \(1.5\ \mathring{A}\), and it must be exactly half rather than three quarters.

Check by direct substitution, with \(m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\) kg: \(E_2 = 600 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 9.6 \times 10^{-17}\) J, so \(p_2 = \sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 9.6 \times 10^{-17}} = 1.322 \times 10^{-23}\) kg m/s and \(\lambda_2 = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{1.322 \times 10^{-23}} = 5.01 \times 10^{-11}\) m \(= 0.501\ \mathring{A}\). The same substitution at \(150\) eV returns \(1.003\ \mathring{A}\), confirming the datum given in the question.
twin: Calculate the wavelength associated with an electron, its momentum and speed (b) when it is moving with kinetic energy of 150 eV.

answer:
**Data:** accelerating potential \(V = 100\) V. Take \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s, \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C and \(m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\) kg.

An electron starting from rest and accelerated through a potential difference \(V\) gains kinetic energy equal to the work done on it by the field:

\(K = eV = (1.6 \times 10^{-19})(100) = 1.6 \times 10^{-17}\) J

Its momentum follows from \(K = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}\):

\(p = \sqrt{2mK} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-17}} = \sqrt{2.915 \times 10^{-47}} = 5.4 \times 10^{-24}\) kg m/s

The de Broglie wavelength is

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\)

\(\therefore\ \lambda = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{5.4 \times 10^{-24}} = 1.228 \times 10^{-10}\) m

\(\therefore\ \lambda = 0.1228\) nm

Check with the compact form obtained by putting the numerical values of \(h\), \(e\) and \(m\) into \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\), namely \(\lambda = \dfrac{1.228}{\sqrt{V \text{ (in volt)}}}\) nm:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{1.228}{\sqrt{100}} = 0.1228\) nm, the same value.
twin: An electron is accelerated through a potential of 120 V. Find its de Broglie wavelength.

answer:
**(B)** electron

For a particle of mass \(m\) and kinetic energy \(K\), the momentum is \(p = \sqrt{2mK}\), so the de Broglie wavelength is

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\)

The four bodies are stated to have the SAME kinetic energy, so \(K\) is common to all of them and

\(\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\)

The longest wavelength therefore belongs to the lightest of the four. Their masses are: electron \(9.11 \times 10^{-31}\) kg; proton \(1.673 \times 10^{-27}\) kg; hydrogen atom \(1.674 \times 10^{-27}\) kg, being a proton with an electron bound to it and so very slightly heavier than the proton; \(\alpha\)-particle \(6.645 \times 10^{-27}\) kg, about four times the proton mass.

The electron is lighter than the proton by a factor of about \(1837\), so its wavelength is longer by \(\sqrt{1837} = 42.9\) times, and it is lighter still than the hydrogen atom and the \(\alpha\)-particle.

\(\therefore\) the electron has the longest associated de Broglie wavelength, while the \(\alpha\)-particle, being the heaviest, has the shortest.

Numerical check at a common \(K = 100\) eV: electron \(1.23\ \mathring{A}\), proton \(0.0287\ \mathring{A}\), hydrogen atom \(0.0286\ \mathring{A}\), \(\alpha\)-particle \(0.0144\ \mathring{A}\). The ordering does not depend on the value chosen for \(K\), since that quantity cancels from every ratio.
